articles.headline: Apple Admits Some $2,000 Folding iPhones Developed Screen Lines, Offers Replacements
articles.dek: Days after launch, Apple says an inner-display issue affects 'a small number' of Duos, and declines to say how small.
articles.catch_up: Apple launched the iPhone Duo, its first foldable and most expensive iPhone, last week at a starting price of £1,999 in the UK. Social media photos soon showed lines on the inner screen, and Apple has now acknowledged a problem.
articles.why_it_matters: Anyone considering a £1,999 phone should know that the first generation of a new hardware category tends to be where the engineering lessons are learned, and the buyers are the ones who pay tuition. Apple's warranty answer matters before 28 more markets get the phone on 30 October.
body: Apple has acknowledged that some iPhone Duo handsets have developed screen problems just days after going on sale, according to the BBC. The company said it was aware of 'an issue impacting the inner display on a small number' of phones and told affected customers to contact it for a replacement. Apple did not say how many devices are affected, which is the part of 'a small number' that most needs a number.

The Duo is Apple's first foldable and the first major iPhone redesign in almost two decades. It starts at £1,999 ($2,668) in the UK and rises to £3,199 for the best-equipped models, making it the most expensive iPhone Apple has sold. Crowds queued at Apple stores around the world last week to buy it.

Photos on social media show lines across the inner display. Some owners also posted images of cracks along the central crease, and others reported a crunching noise when opening the phone. One user, Justin Lokos, posted a picture of a faulty unit and later one of a replacement, thanking an Apple store in New York.

A note of caution is in order. The BBC reported that some of the images of faulty devices may have been created using AI. Translation: in 2025-era internet terms, a photo of a broken phone is now a claim rather than evidence, which is awkward for both critics and defenders.

Francisco Jeronimo, an analyst at IDC, said the caveat means people should be careful about drawing conclusions about the whole production run. He also said the early reports show 'that even a company with Apple's engineering resources and supply chain discipline faces a steep learning curve in foldables'. That is a polite way of saying that folding glass is hard, even for a company worth trillions.

The hinge is the culprit in the general theory. The Duo's 7.6-inch inner display is held together by a central hinge, a piece of engineering that has caused similar flaws in rivals' folding phones. Samsung's first foldable, the Galaxy Fold, ran into broken-screen reports from reviewers in 2019. Apple spent years developing the technology while Android users enjoyed a broad selection of foldables, and its reward is that it now gets to rediscover the same hinge.

Ars Technica's review was more favourable on the hardware. Reviewer Andrew Cunningham said Apple has wrangled the crease 'so close to invisibility' that he rarely thought about it. His complaints were elsewhere: he called the Duo technically impressive but not always enjoyable, said it works well as a small iPad, and could not name a way he prefers it to a regular iPhone. He also noted it lacks Face ID and a customizable Action Button.

The business stakes are larger than one batch of screens. Jeronimo said that because Apple pitched the Duo as a 'premium alternative' to existing foldables, how it handles this problem will shape buyer confidence in the whole category. He added that Apple's loyal customers and retail network, which can swap devices on the spot, are an advantage, but that it needs to clarify its warranty position quickly.

New chief executive John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September, said last month that the Duo would 'redefine the experience of using a foldable phone'. Early evidence suggests it has redefined the experience of visiting an Apple Store in the first week. What to watch is whether Apple publishes a number, and what its warranty says, before the next 28 markets open on 30 October.
articles.wire_headline: Apple to replace iPhone Duos affected by screen problem

articles.headline: U.S. Borrows $2 Trillion a Year, Finds Lenders Want 5% to Keep Answering the Phone
articles.dek: With a $1.992 trillion deficit and the 10-year Treasury near 5.1%, higher borrowing costs are reaching mortgages, while AI giants borrow just as eagerly and investors call it a bargain.
articles.catch_up: The U.S. government ran a deficit of $1.992 trillion in fiscal 2026, and long-term Treasury yields have climbed about 114 basis points since the Iran war began on Feb. 28. Meanwhile, tech giants are issuing record amounts of debt to fund AI infrastructure.
articles.why_it_matters: Treasury yields set the price of mortgages, so the 10-year near 5% means the cost of buying a home and of servicing federal debt both rise. Investors, meanwhile, are being offered high yields on AI-linked corporate bonds, along with a concentrated bet on the AI story.
body: The U.S. government ran a deficit of $1.992 trillion in the 2026 fiscal year, up 12% from last year, according to Treasury data cited by CNBC. That is roughly 6.2% of gross domestic product. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued the country should aim for under 4% by the end of President Trump's term, a target CNBC describes as almost impossible to hit. It is a goal in the way a gym membership in January is a goal.

The 10-year Treasury yield traded at 5.1% on Friday, up 114 basis points since the end of February. Translation: a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so the government's borrowing cost rose by about 1.14 percentage points in eight months. CNBC attributes the rise partly to the war with Iran, which lifted oil and diesel prices and made bond traders ask for more yield in case the Federal Reserve has to raise rates.

The second cause is supply. Investors want extra compensation for holding long-term bonds because they expect the government to keep issuing them. They also face competition from companies selling hundreds of billions in debt to build AI infrastructure. Translation: the Treasury is no longer the only borrower with a shopping cart and a deadline, and lenders have noticed they can be choosy.

Ordinary people feel this through mortgages, which track the 10-year yield. The average 30-year fixed rate is hovering around 7.5%, and Redfin said pending home sales fell 4% in September, the biggest monthly drop in three years. The government borrows at 5.1% and the household at 7.5%, which is what economists call a spread and what buyers call a reason to keep renting.

Higher rates also feed back into the deficit. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that rates a half-point above its forecast would add $1.9 trillion to deficits over ten years, and 1.5 points above would add $6 trillion. The CBO expects the 10-year to average 4.3%, versus 5.1% today. Bessent's answer is growth: 'we have to grow our way out of it,' he said in Dallas. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget calculates that this would take a decade of 7.2% growth. Second-quarter growth was recently revised up to 2.2%.

Politics offers little relief. Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House in the Nov. 3 midterms, and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker, wants to reverse $1 trillion in healthcare cuts. Trump, for his part, pledged $5,000 checks to every adult citizen if Republicans swept the election, which is a distinctive approach to deficit reduction. CNBC notes that divided government sometimes yields surprising compromises, but the starting points are far apart.

Meanwhile, the other big borrowers are having a fine time. CNBC reports that hyperscalers such as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are leading corporate issuance, and the VettaFi AI Hyperscaler Bond Index yielded 6.51% at the end of September. Hyperscalers issued $93 billion of debt in 2025, against an annual average of about $35 billion from 2020 to 2024. Some fixed-income experts call it a 'generational opportunity.' TCW's Steven Purdy said such highly rated companies typically cannot be bought at these yields.

There are caveats, which the experts supplied themselves. Meta's free cash flow turned negative for the first time since its 2012 IPO, and the company announced plans to sell up to $95 billion of stock as well. Oracle's debt was downgraded in July to the lowest tier of investment grade, and CoreWeave's bonds fell in October. JPMorgan forecast in June that more than $4 trillion of AI-related debt could be issued through 2030. Cerity's Joseph Matus warned that most investors already own these companies through stocks, so the bonds add yield but not much diversification.

So the picture is two enormous borrowers, one government and one industry, each promising that growth will cover the bill. CNBC notes that expensive borrowing is not the same as a crisis, and that higher yields are also drawing buyers to Treasuries. The next test is whether the politics can be fixed before the arithmetic needs it. The first checkpoint is Nov. 3.
articles.wire_headline: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge

articles.headline: Britain's New Chancellor Taxes Banks, Praises Banks, and Asks Banks to Understand
articles.dek: John Healey's first budget lifts the bank surcharge to 6% for 15 months, cuts household energy costs and pledges £10 billion to Ukraine, and bank shares rose anyway.
articles.catch_up: Britain's finance minister John Healey delivered his first Autumn Budget on Wednesday under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, with inflation at 3.5% and borrowing costs elevated. He cited the impact of the U.S.-Iran war on fuel prices as a reason for the cost-of-living measures.
articles.why_it_matters: The budget shows how a government with high borrowing costs and rising defense commitments pays for relief: it taxes the one sector that can absorb it and hopes markets stay calm. Households get lower energy bills, while the rest of the bill is deferred to a spending review next year.
body: John Healey, Britain's finance minister, delivered his first budget on Wednesday, announcing help with energy bills, a higher tax on banks, and more money for defense and Ukraine. According to CNBC, markets responded broadly positively, which is the highest grade a chancellor can receive and one that is usually revoked within a few weeks.

The backdrop is unglamorous. Inflation rose to 3.5% in September, driven by fuel costs, and CNBC reported that markets expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates next month. Healey blamed part of the pressure on the U.S.-Iran war, a conflict he said Britain did not want. Translation: Britain imports energy, so it pays for other countries' disagreements at the gas meter.

The relief package is broad. Standing charges on household gas heating bills will be removed, a tax break on electricity is extended through July 2027, and £100 checks go to households in the four lowest local housing tax bands, at a cost of £2.6 billion. Tariffs come off more than 100 grocery products, the minimum wage rises 3.9%, and a planned cut to tax-free savings thresholds was canceled. Translation: standing charges are the fixed fee you pay for the privilege of being connected, before you have used anything.

To pay for it, Healey said he would raise money from those who can afford it, while promising no tax rises on wages or dividends. Banks, gambling businesses and vape shops will pay. The bank surcharge rises by 3 points to 6% from January and lasts 15 months. Healey had earlier this month called the banks a jewel in Britain's economic crown, and he described them on Wednesday as making a huge contribution. Translation: he complimented the patient before the invoice.

The sector appeared to have expected worse. CNBC reported that Barclays rose 3.3%, Lloyds more than 2.6% and NatWest 2.5%. JPMorgan Chase was less relaxed, saying that singling out the industry for additional taxes again lacks principle. CEO Jamie Dimon has previously suggested the bank might rethink its Canary Wharf headquarters buildout if the government is hostile, though the company said Wednesday it is committed to the U.K.

On defense, Healey set a 2030 target date for spending of 3% of GDP and reaffirmed the NATO pledge of 3.5% by 2035. He announced £10 billion in economic and military support for Ukraine, built on loans and export finance guarantees, plus £500 million in urgent military funding for this winter. He also announced £2.5 billion for a Rolls-Royce engine partnership. IG analyst Chris Beauchamp said the announcement lacked detail but that the spending bonanza for Rolls-Royce and others is still on the way, only slowly.

The numbers around it were tidy. The Office for Budget Responsibility forecast £15 billion of fiscal headroom by 2029/30, debt rising slightly to 83.8% of GDP next year, then falling to 81.7% by 2032, and growth of 1.2% this year. Translation: headroom is the cushion between what the government plans to borrow and what its own rules allow, and it is the figure markets watch to decide whether to panic. Ten-year gilt yields fell 2 basis points to 5.323%, which is still a rate that makes a finance minister choose his words carefully.

Healey also promised to cut the welfare bill, which hit 10.7% of GDP in 2024/25, while saying he would not write off a million young people. His predecessor watered down similar plans after a rebellion in her own party. The details of paying for defense are left to next year's spending review, which is where the actual choices tend to appear.
articles.wire_headline: The UK cuts energy bills, taxes banks and boosts defense in high-stakes budget

articles.headline: Nelson Peltz Offers $1.4 Billion to Take Wendy's Private, Citing Need for Money
articles.dek: A Trian-led group bids $7.35 a share, a 20% premium, for a burger chain whose stock is down 65% in two years and which, by its own largest shareholder's account, needs a lot more cash.
articles.catch_up: Wendy's has reported six straight quarters of falling same-store sales and has cycled through several chief executives. On Wednesday, a regulatory filing showed Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management leading a group offering to buy the company outright.
articles.why_it_matters: If the deal goes ahead, a publicly traded fast-food chain would move its turnaround out of quarterly earnings view, which says something about how hard cheap burgers have become to sell profitably. For shareholders, the offer is a rare exit at a premium after a long slide.
body: A group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management has offered $1.4 billion to take Wendy's private, according to a regulatory filing reported by CNBC on Wednesday. The price is $7.35 per share in cash, a 20% premium to Tuesday's closing price. Shares rose about 15% in morning trading, which is the market's way of saying it would like the offer to be real.

The group includes Trian, BlueFive Capital, Sixth Street Partners and Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees. Translation: a franchisee, the people who actually run the restaurants, has joined the people who own the stock, in the hope of becoming the people who own the company. Trian and affiliated parties already hold 16.25% of Wendy's, according to the filing, making them its largest shareholder. The Wall Street Journal first reported the proposal.

The filing, MarketWatch noted, says the company "requires significant capital investment" to get back on track. That is an unusual sales pitch from a buyer, equivalent to telling a seller the house is lovely and also needs a roof, plumbing and a plan. It also suggests the overhaul will be expensive, and that Trian would prefer to pay for it without analysts watching.

The backdrop is not subtle. Wendy's stock has fallen 65% over two years, even counting Wednesday's gain, and same-store sales, the measure of how much more or less each existing restaurant sells, have declined for six straight quarters. Budget-conscious diners are eating out less, and Wendy's and its rivals have answered with discounts, which draw customers in while shrinking what each one is worth.

Leadership has not helped. CNBC described a revolving door of chief executives with differing ideas about the turnaround. The newest, Bob Wright, joined in May from Potbelly, which itself went private. On his first earnings call in August, he was candid about muddled value offerings, inconsistent restaurant execution and too many one-off promotions. Fixing all three is the sort of work that looks better when nobody is grading you every 90 days.

TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles agreed with the logic, writing that a take-private makes sense because the turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the state of the lower-income consumer and the soft burger category. Take-private, for the uninitiated, means buying all the public shares and delisting the company, so that losses can be endured in relative privacy.

There is history here. Peltz led an activist campaign at Wendy's more than two decades ago, and Trian explored a takeover in 2022 before deciding against it. A 65% drop in the share price has a way of changing one's mind about the asking price. Wendy's did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment, and Trian declined to comment beyond the filing.

The next date to watch is Nov. 5, when Wendy's reports third-quarter earnings before the market opens. If sales fell again, it would be a seventh consecutive data point in favor of the buyers' argument about the price.
articles.wire_headline: Wendy’s buyout offer suggests the burger chain’s overhaul could be very expensive

articles.headline: Fed Expected to Do Nothing This Week, Then Something Later, Say People Paid to Guess
articles.dek: A CNBC survey finds 93% of 30 forecasters expect a pause now and 76% expect a hike in December, with 10-year yields sitting around 5%.
articles.catch_up: The Federal Reserve meets this week, with inflation at 3.7% and oil prices elevated by the war in Iran. CNBC surveys fund managers, strategists and economists before every Fed meeting, and the latest edition polled 30 of them.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher rates mean costlier mortgages, car loans and credit cards, while a Fed that waits too long risks letting inflation settle in. The forecasters mostly expect the pain to be postponed, not cancelled.
body: The Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its meeting this week, according to CNBC's latest Fed Survey. Of the 30 fund managers, strategists and economists polled, 93% expect a pause. That is about as close to consensus as economics gets, a field where people usually disagree over the definition of the word 'recession.'

The consensus ends there. Seventy-six percent expect a rate hike at the December meeting, and more than half expect the Fed to raise rates next year by an average of about two hikes. Translation: the Fed will not raise rates today, but respondents think it will be raising them soon, which is the central banking equivalent of saying you will start the diet on Monday.

Some respondents think Monday has already come and gone. Richard Bernstein of Janus Henderson called the Fed's hesitancy 'unfathomable,' pointing to nominal GDP running 6-8% and uniformly warm-to-hot inflation indicators. Translation: nominal GDP is growth before subtracting inflation, so a big number there can mean the economy is expanding or merely that everything costs more. John Ryding of Brean Capital wrote that demand and inflation data point to a strong need to hike. Thirty percent said the Fed should hike at this meeting, and survey respondents expect at least two Fed voters to dissent from holding steady.

The other camp is led by Mark Zandi of Moody's Analytics, who cited the intensifying Iran war, falling real wages, rising interest rates and a shaky AI-fueled stock market. 'Inflation is high, but there's little sign it is becoming entrenched,' he wrote. Translation: entrenched inflation is when businesses and workers start assuming prices will keep rising and act accordingly, which makes it self-fulfilling and very annoying to remove.

The survey's broader numbers describe an economy that is being told to brace while continuing to behave. Respondents see GDP growth of 2.4% this year, above the 2.2% they see as potential for 2027, and put recession odds at 26%, down from 29%. Unemployment is expected to stay at 4.2% before rising to 4.4% in 2027. The Consumer Price Index is forecast at 3.6%, falling to 2.6% next year. Forty percent say the Fed must slow growth below potential to fix inflation, which is a polite way of saying the cure involves making the economy somewhat worse on purpose.

Oil complicates the story. Respondents forecast the U.S. crude benchmark at $88 a barrel in six months, below the current $101 cited by CNBC. Seventy percent say inflation is broader than energy prices. Official data show Brent crude at 123.1 as of Oct. 27, so anyone relying on a falling-oil forecast is making a confident bet against the thing currently happening.

Then there are bond yields. Respondents split almost evenly on the cause: inflation, growth, heavy debt issuance and expectations of higher Fed rates. Asked about supply, 50% blamed government debt, 13% blamed borrowing to fund the AI buildout, and a third said both contributed equally. The 10-year Treasury yield stood at 5.0% in the latest official data, and respondents see it staying above 5% this year. Subodh Kumar called yields above 5% 'a new band, not an anomaly.' Translation: the government's borrowing costs have moved up a floor, and nobody is bringing the old furniture back.

Politics gets a turn as well. Sixty-three percent see some market risk from legal challenges that could drag out the question of who controls Congress after next week's election. More than half now expect Democratic control of both houses, up from 29% last time, and 40% expect Democrats to take the House but not the Senate. Yet respondents see little change in taxes and little difference in growth forecasts by party, which suggests the markets fear the uncertainty far more than the outcome.

The biggest risks named were the continuation of the Iran war and a burst AI bubble. Rob Morgan of MOSAIC suggested the Fed chair tell the president that the quickest way to lower inflation is ending tariffs and the war. It is a tidy policy proposal that sits outside the Fed's authority, which may be why it was offered by a strategist and not a voter. For now, the Fed holds, the forecasters wait for December, and the 10-year yield stays where it is.
articles.wire_headline: Fed rate hikes are coming, but not this week: CNBC survey

articles.headline: Stellantis Shares Jump 12% After Losing Slightly Less Cash Than Feared
articles.dek: The Chrysler and Jeep owner posted a 1% revenue gain and reaffirmed its 2026 guidance, which on a bad year counts as a triumph.
articles.catch_up: Stellantis, the European automaker behind Chrysler and Jeep, announced a 60 billion euro turnaround plan in May under CEO Antonio Filosa. On Wednesday it reported third-quarter results, its latest check on whether that plan is working.
articles.why_it_matters: Investors are watching whether legacy automakers can fix their finances while Chinese rivals take market share. If Stellantis hits its cash-flow target, it suggests the turnaround is real; if not, the 60 billion euros starts to look like a very large bet.
body: Stellantis shares rose roughly 9% in Milan on Wednesday and were up 12% in early New York trading, after the company reported third-quarter revenue of 37.6 billion euros, up 1% from a year earlier, according to CNBC. Adjusted operating income rose 184% to 256 million euros from 90 million. The company, in other words, grew sales by roughly the amount a rounding error would, and investors responded as if it had found oil.

The 184% figure deserves context. Translation: when profit starts from 90 million euros on a business that size, almost any improvement looks heroic in percentage terms. Industrial free cash flow, meaning the cash the car-making business generates after paying for its operations and investments, improved to negative 4 billion euros from negative 4.3 billion. That is still negative 4 billion euros, but it is a more tasteful negative.

The real news was what Stellantis did not do. It reconfirmed its 2026 guidance, which includes a mid-single-digit increase in net revenue, a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin and a target of positive free cash flow next year. RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan wrote that the third quarter was soft but expectations were far lower, and that guidance held while other automakers and suppliers are cutting on elevated costs. Translation: the bar was on the floor, and the company stepped over it.

Filosa told investors the company is ahead of schedule on the plan and expects to beat its earlier 6 billion euro cost-cutting target by 2028, including 2.4 billion euros to start 2027. Pressed on whether the cash-flow target is realistic, he said, "We are very confident in reaffirming our '26 guidance." Investors have heard confident statements before, but this one came with a number attached, which is the preferred format.

The longer plan involves investing 36 billion euros across its brands, with 60% going to the struggling North American business. It also aims to lift revenue about 23%, from 154 billion euros last year to 190 billion euros by 2030, with a 7% adjusted operating margin. Today's margin target is low single digits, so the company is promising to roughly double or triple its profitability while selling more cars in a market that is not asking for them.

The backdrop is China, where CNBC noted Xiaomi, BYD and Geely are gaining ground against European brands. Porsche said this week it would reduce its China exposure, and Mercedes-Benz blamed a slump in third-quarter sales there on a challenging market environment. Filosa, for his part, has asked European regulators to reward carmakers that actually design and engineer cars in the region, a request that is both a policy position and a polite description of the competition.

The stock's jump should be kept in proportion. CNBC noted it remains sharply down since the start of the year, so Wednesday's rally recovers some ground rather than reaching new territory. The next test is whether a company that is burning 4 billion euros can turn cash-positive in 2027, a promise with a very clear deadline.
articles.wire_headline: Stellantis stock rises 12% as automaker's turnaround plan, cost cuts gain traction
